meta.headline: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

relevance.reason: A central bank interest rate decision, inflation above target and the effects on borrowers link directly to monetary policy and the role of central banks.

mapping.justification: The main issue is whether the Bank of England should change interest rates, which is monetary policy, a demand-side policy.
mapping.cross_theme_note: The article spans Theme 2 (inflation and monetary policy) and Theme 4 (the role of central banks, including bond purchases and sales).

paragraphs: The Bank of England has left its main interest rate at 3.75% for the sixth time in a row, but its governor, Andrew Bailey, said energy price volatility makes a future rise more likely. The war involving Iran has disrupted global energy supplies, causing sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.

Inflation reached 3.1% in August and has been above the Bank's 2% target for nearly two years. The Bank now expects it to be slightly above 4% early next year. Of the nine members of the Monetary Policy Committee, six voted to hold rates and three, including the chief economist, wanted a rise to 4%.

There was some good news. The UK economy has been more resilient than expected, and the Bank raised its growth forecast for July to September from 0.1% to 0.4%. Food price inflation is now expected to reach 4% by the end of the year rather than 6% to 7%, because higher energy costs have not yet spread widely through the economy.

Markets expect higher rates, so lenders have already raised mortgage costs. The average two-year fixed rate is 5.77% and the five-year rate is 5.83%. One borrower expects to pay about £300 more a month when a 1.19% deal ends.

The Bank also paused its quantitative tightening programme, choosing to sell its £488bn stock of bonds in smaller amounts over eight years. Yields on UK government bonds fell after the announcement, which lowers the government's borrowing costs.

The Bank of England's interest rate decisions affect the cost of borrowing for households, firms and the government. This article shows the central bank balancing inflation above its target against the risk of slowing an economy that is growing more strongly than expected. It also shows that interest rates are a blunt tool when inflation is driven by higher energy costs from abroad.

concepts: Inflation target and the Monetary Policy Committee
Transmission of interest rate changes to spending and investment
Bond yields and the cost of government borrowing
chain: A war involving Iran disrupts energy supplies, raising fuel and energy costs for firms and households.
Higher costs shift short-run aggregate supply to the left, causing cost-push inflation of 3.1%, above the 2% target.
The MPC may raise Bank rate to stop inflation staying high, and lenders have already raised mortgage rates.
Higher borrowing costs reduce households' disposable income and firms' investment, so AD shifts left.
Lower demand eases price pressure, but the problem is on the supply side, so higher rates treat the symptom and risk lower growth.
Separately, pausing QT means fewer bonds are sold, which lowers bond yields and eases the government's borrowing costs.

evaluation.label: Type of inflation
evaluation.text: the pressure comes mainly from energy costs on the supply side, so raising interest rates may do little to reduce it and could slow growth.

evaluation.label: Time lags
evaluation.text: interest rate changes take time to work, and the Bank says the effect of energy costs on the wider economy is still being assessed, so waiting for more information is a reasonable choice.

evaluation.label: Who is affected
evaluation.text: mortgage borrowers face higher payments and savers may gain, while the government benefits if bond yields fall.

key_terms.definition: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences the interest rates that banks charge and pay.
The group at the Bank of England that votes on the level of Bank rate to meet the inflation target.
The rate of inflation the central bank aims to achieve, which is 2% in the UK.
A rise in the general price level caused by higher costs of production, such as energy or raw materials.
When a central bank creates money to buy assets such as government bonds, in order to lower long-term interest rates and support spending.
When a central bank reduces the stock of assets it bought, for example by selling government bonds.
The return an investor receives on a bond, which rises when bond prices fall and reflects the government's cost of borrowing.
A home loan where the interest rate stays the same for an agreed period, such as two or five years.
The total planned spending on an economy's goods and services, made up of consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.

questions.prompt: Explain one way a rise in interest rates could help to reduce inflation.

points: Identifies that higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing or reward saving.
Uses the article, for example the two-year fixed mortgage rate of 5.77%, the borrower paying about £300 more a month, or inflation of 3.1% against a 2% target.

Develops a chain, for example: higher mortgage and loan costs reduce households' disposable income and spending, and firms cut investment (1), so aggregate demand falls and there is less upward pressure on prices (1).

questions.prompt: Assess whether the Bank of England should raise interest rates.

points: Higher Bank rate raises borrowing costs and lowers consumption, investment and aggregate demand.
Inflation of 3.1% and above target for nearly two years.
Forecast of slightly above 4% early next year.
Three of nine MPC members wanted 4%.
For a rise: prevents inflation expectations becoming embedded, brings inflation back to target, and other central banks such as the Fed and the ECB have already raised rates.

Against a rise: the inflation comes from energy costs abroad, so higher rates do little to fix it; borrowers face higher payments; higher rates could weaken growth, and food price inflation is now forecast lower than before.
Judge using the cause of inflation, the time lag before a rise takes effect, how far energy costs will spread and whether the conflict continues.
A supported conclusion might be that the Bank is right to wait, provided it signals it will act if inflation spreads to wages and other prices.
